content: Perineal trauma is a significant issue that affects millions of women globally each year. The pain and discomfort associated with perineal trauma are often underestimated. This pain can interfere with essential daily activities such as walking, sitting, and urinating, and it can also negatively impact a woman’s experience of motherhood. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of topically applied anaesthetics in relieving perineal pain after childbirth, both during the hospital stay and after discharge. To achieve this, a search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of June 2007. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared topically applied anaesthetics with no treatment, placebo, or alternative treatments. Eight trials involving a total of 976 women were included in the analysis. Five of these trials assessed pain relief within the first 24 hours after childbirth, but each study used different methods to measure pain. None of these trials demonstrated a significant difference in pain relief when topical anaesthetics were compared to placebo. One study compared topical anaesthetics with indomethacin vaginal suppositories and found no significant difference in mean pain scores. All the included trials only reported short-term follow-up, lasting up to four days. Two trials examined the use of additional analgesia for perineal pain. One trial found that women who used epifoam required less additional analgesia compared to those who received a placebo (relative risk [RR] 0.58, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.40 to 0.84; one trial, 97 women). However, lignocaine (lidocaine) did not show any difference in the need for additional analgesia. Adverse effects were not systematically measured in the included studies. However, some studies noted that there were no side effects severe enough to warrant discontinuation of treatment. One study reported that women in the treatment group were more satisfied with their care compared to those in the placebo group (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.65; one trial, 103 women). In conclusion, the evidence supporting the effectiveness of topically applied local anaesthetics for managing perineal pain after childbirth is not strong. Additionally, the long-term effects of these treatments have not been evaluated.
